toc.title: Coming out of freeze in the moment
Coming out of freeze through thawing

blocks.p: Your autonomic nervous system has three primary states: [safety](piece:safety-state), [flight/fight](piece:flight-fight-state) and [shutdown](piece:shutdown-state). There are also mixed states. When two (or all) primary states are active simultaneously, they create a mixed state. If you mix two primary colors, you get a secondary color, right? Red paint mixed with blue paint makes purple paint. Two primaries create a mixed result. Same with Polyvagal primary states.
The mixed-state equations are as follows:

You've probably noticed by now that I refer to the third Polyvagal rung as "shutdown" and not "freeze." Typically, the word "freeze" is used and was also my default word. That is, until I chatted with Dr. Porges and he clarified that "freeze" and "shutdown" are distinct autonomic phenomena, though closely connected. "There is this whole ambiguity because people use the word 'freeze' when they really mean 'shutting down.' The mouse in the jaws of a cat is not frozen, it's just limp... The limp loss of muscle tone is a dorsal vagal response."

Shutdown and freeze are both immobile, though shutdown is a limp collapse, and freeze is tense. Freeze combines sympathetic flight/fight arousal plus dorsal vagal shutdown, mobility plus immobility. Freeze involves an intense and rapid buildup of energy to run or fight while simultaneously the body immobilizes due to force or perception.
Sexual assault is an obvious example: there is an impulse to mobilize, but the individual is unable to use it. They enter a freeze mixed state. Their body is immobile while sympathetically charged.

People can also enter the freeze state in everyday scenarios like being put to sleep while highly anxious before surgery. When someone goes under in this state, they come out of their anesthesia with a sympathetic charge. They wake up in a fit, screaming or flailing. This terrifying waking scenario is something that medical staff have told me they often witness in surgical rooms.

Panic may be the most common experience of freeze. Think about the last time you had a panic attack: your heart rate was probably increased, breathing shallow and pressured, but you were also immobile. Your sympathetic state was active, but frozen.

Phobias may be the result of a freeze response within individuals. Certain stimuli, such as spiders, activate the sympathetic and dorsal vagal systems. For me, driving over bridges can induce this response, especially if I can't see the ground. Rationally, I know I'm safe: my car is reliable, I'm a capable driver, and the bridge is structurally sound (isn't it?). However, when I cross over those bridges, my heart rate goes up, breathing becomes shallow and rapid, and muscles tense. Despite my efforts to stay grounded, I feel disconnected from reality. My mind conjures a catastrophic scenario where my car stalls on the bridge, causing a pile-up.

After talking out loud, narrating everything happening, and forcing myself to maintain regular breathing, I overcome the freeze response and regain control. Once I reach solid ground, the freeze immediately subsides.

Freeze is the combination of sympathetic flight/fight plus shutdown. But the sympathetic system has two distinct possibilities: flight and fight. What happens when one is in a dominant flight sympathetic plus shutdown? And what about a dominant fight plus shutdown?

When flight mixes with shutdown, it results in a frozen panic (like with phobias). Panic is specifically the immobilized impulse to flee. But when fight mixes with shutdown, it results in explosive rage. At least, the release of the fight activation from a fight freeze can be rage when the immobilization comes off.

blocks.h: Coming out of freeze in the moment

blocks.p: There isn't a singular coping skill that works for everyone in the intense moments of panic, rage, or overwhelm. (Sorry to say.) Sensory stimulation is helpful for some. It may help if a loved one firmly grasps your hand. Saying things aloud can be helpful, like narrating what is happening or counting things in the environment. Anything to get grounded in your body and activate the safety pathways enough for the defensive flight/fight and shutdown pathways to recede.

These and many many other options are fairly typical coping skills or grounding techniques to reduce the intensity of a momentary freeze. They don't exactly help the individual to feel safe; more like they reduce the freeze activation. Coping with freeze is different than anchoring into safety and balancing it out.

It may seem impossible, but if you build the strength of your safety state enough, you can eventually notice when there is a tolerable amount of panic in the system, before it becomes overwhelming. You may notice it as anxiety or worry. The feeling is present, but it has not yet built into a crescendo of panic. Likewise, you could eventually notice lower levels of anger or irritation before they build into rage. Or, mild stress before it becomes overwhelm.

When you notice the lower level of emotions building into freeze, you can use mindful safety anchoring or coping skills more effectively. Balance out the mild freeze with safety activation. When you do, the immobilization of freeze can recede, allowing the mobility of flight/fight. Then, mindfully use the flight/fight activation through mobility, like walking outside or tensing and releasing your muscles. It can also help to listen to and allow your body to breathe as it naturally needs to, or purposefully extend your exhale.

This probably seems impossible. Intimidating. If you practice safety outside the context of a freeze, using those same skills is more accessible. Likewise, practice noticing mild flight/fight activation before it becomes anxiety or anger that is too much. When you notice it, use a safety practice to balance it out. Over time, your ability to notice mild freeze activation early on will increase and you can use coping or safety anchoring techniques more effectively. Freeze activation will also reduce and be more tolerable. Eventually, it may not be an issue at all.

blocks.why: Practice safety outside the context of a freeze, so it is there when you need it. This practice does that.

blocks.h: Coming out of freeze through thawing

blocks.p: But a freeze state can be ongoing: not just a panic attack, but a state that someone can potentially exist in for years and years. Don't confront the long-lasting freeze directly. Instead, one should gradually thaw the freeze. Ideally, the stuck sympathetic energy is felt in small pieces at a time, something called [titration](piece:vagal-brake#titration).

However, therapists and other helping professionals often ignore one essential aspect of thawing a freeze in their trauma work: building the client's safety state strength. This neglect results in re-traumatization. If your safety state is not strong enough, you may end up retraumatizing yourself by attempting to heal your freeze before you're ready for it. It will be self-defeating and reinforce any fears you have about getting unstuck.

I know you want to discharge your freeze energy, heal the trauma, and move on with life. Like, right now. But don't rush this process because it could result in re-traumatization. Therapies that focus on trauma narratives, like EMDR and Trauma-Focused Cognitive Behavioral Therapy, may inadvertently reinforce trauma due to this reason.

Titration (releasing a bit of trauma at a time) becomes an option once you anchor deeply enough into safety. Part of titration is another process called pendulation: shifting from safety to defense and then back to safety. Pendulation repeats until the defensive state softens enough to be tolerable or even discharges from the body.

blocks.prompt: When was the last time you felt tense, overwhelmed, apprehensive, or stressed? Do you think those were mild or moderate freeze activations? How could you tell?
Have you tried therapies or other interventions that reinforced the freeze? How could you tell?
Do you feel more like rushing through trauma recovery or being patient? Has this changed over time?

q: "We are biologically programmed to freeze (or go limp) when flight or fight is either impossible or perceived to be impossible. Freeze and collapse are the last-ditch, "default" responses to an inescapable threat, even if that threat is a microbe in our blood." (Levine)
